See what’s trending and how to recognize red flags.
Stopping scams is everyone’s responsibility. Together, we can help keep your accounts protected.
Don’t click links in emails or reply to texts about an “unpaid toll”
Review quick tips to help protect your money
Always use verified sites and watch out for offers that sound too good to be true
Scam details change, but red flags remain the same. Even if a story seems to make sense, verify the information through a trusted source.
Scammers may pretend to be someone you trust, like an official, someone from a familiar organization, a bank employee, a friend or a family member.
They may tell you stories to make you feel fear, sympathy or love. They may urge you to ignore your instincts or lie about why you’re moving money.
Scammers may say there’s a problem that needs immediate attention to make you act before you think and rush you into making hasty decisions without consulting anyone you trust.
They may offer money, a job, or a prize, make claims of an emergency, or threaten you with legal action or notifying law enforcement.
They may tell you not to trust Bank of America employees, say to ignore warning messages or coach you on what to say — including to lie.
Scammers may tell you to send money or payment in less common ways, such as a wire transfer, gift cards or non-traditional forms of payment like gold, cryptocurrency or pre-loaded debit cards.
Imposters are real, but their requests are not. Their goal is to deceive. Yours is to detect — and protect.
Don’t rush. If someone asks for money or personal info and it feels off, trust your instincts and don’t engage.
Even if the request appears legitimate, talk it over with someone you trust - like a friend or family member - or call a trusted and known number like from your card or statement.
Create complex passwords, use multi-factor authentication and biometrics like Face ID to help prevent and protect from scams.

Every year, data breaches expose millions of records. Cybercrime costs the global economy trillions of dollars, and the threat landscape changes as criminals exploit new gaps in the expanding digital space.
Managing these risks requires acquiring or building the right tools, and then putting them in the hands of the most innovative and committed cybersecurity teams.
These teams are equipped with a top-to-bottom view of our operations and the information we use, as well as a robust framework that allows them to respond at any time.
Bank of America is deeply committed to protecting our company and our client's information and assets from persistent and emerging cybersecurity threats.

We're also creating new dynamic cybersecurity solutions that help our colleagues and our clients around the globe prepare for, prevent, detect, mitigate, and then respond to and recover from cyber events.
We're invested in powerful cutting-edge technology to ensure that our more than 3,600 cybersecurity teammates have global reach and always-on visibility into our network and our operations.

We look inward as well as outward. Our cybersecurity processes and guidelines cover our internal operations, and we're constantly designing new ways to keep the criminals out, detecting them before they exploit vulnerabilities and containing incidents while improving defenses through our collective experiences.
Our cybersecurity team collaborates to create new strategies for data protection, regulatory compliance, and third-party management, while always staying vigilant against cybercrime.

The Bank's Global Information Security program brings together some of cybersecurity's brightest talents. People with diverse backgrounds and deep experience across a variety of traditional and non-traditional industries. We all benefit when established leaders in the field work together with the sharpest minds across generations.

Our customers and clients are innovating, breaking new ground, and solving problems constantly. The Global Information Security team at Bank of America provides the comprehensive security and insights they need to succeed.

We are better when we're together. With the right framework, tools and people, we're able to be always on to engage in the present while preparing for the future and empowering our customers and clients with the confidence to set and attain their most ambitious goals in today's dynamic and digital marketplace.

Cybercriminals are getting crafty on social media—using posts to trick you into sharing personal info or even money. Consider keeping profiles private, avoid suspicious links and never share sensitive details in posts, comments or direct messages.

Scammers post fake listings, advertise unreal low prices or sell counterfeit goods. They often demand upfront payment — then vanish, leaving you empty-handed. Ensure you verify sellers and use secure payment methods.

Imposters pose as bankers, advisors or other trusted figures using fake phone numbers, websites, emails and social media to steal your info. They may access your accounts or open products in your name. Verify who you’re talking to and don’t click links.

Imagine showing up to your new home or vacation rental to find out it doesn't exist. Scammers may take over listings and change contact information. Book through trusted platforms and verify the listing and owner.

Scammers may pose as recruiters, promising high pay for little effort, pressuring you to respond fast. They may ask for money upfront or send an advance but ask for part of the money back. Always research companies.

“Investment managers” who contact you with news of “opportunities” promising to double your money or guarantee returns are almost always scams. Be skeptical of get-rich-quick offers and never share info with strangers.

Scammers use dating apps and social media to build trust fast — then exploit it with emotional pleas that end in requests for money. Don’t send money to someone you’ve only met online and be cautious of urgent or emotional requests.

A pop-up warning, with a convenient tech support number, is likely a scam. These fake warnings are designed to scare you, and the unsolicited support could cause you to lose money. Close the pop-up immediately and don’t call the number.

Bank of America does not sell personal information, but we may share personal information for targeted advertising. You have the right to opt-out of the selling or sharing of your personal information.

By switching the toggle to the left and clicking save, you are indicating that you do not want us to sell your personal information or share your personal information for online targeted advertising activities.

If you do not have an account or if you are not logged into your account, your request to opt-out of sale/sharing will be linked to your browser identifier only and not linked to any account information because the connection between your browser and the account is not known to us.

At any time, you may change your preference setting using the toggle bar.  Any manual adjustment will override previous settings.

Bank of America does not sell your Personal Information. Beginning in April 2025, we have commenced sharing Personal Information collected from our webpages with non-affiliated, third-party websites and advertisers to provide a personalized marketing experience, commonly known as Cross-context Behavioral Advertising. 
 
Bank of America customers can request to opt-out from the sharing of their Personal Information for cross-context behavioral advertising. 
 
How to opt-out of sharing your information: 
We offer two (2) methods for opting out:

 1. Click “Your Privacy Choices” link at the bottom of our web and mobile pages. On the pop-up window, select the “Sharing and Selling of Personal Data” tab located in the left column. Here you will be able to choose your preferences. Note: you can make changes to your preferences at any time; any adjustment will override the previous settings. 
 2. Using your web browser. Bank of America recognizes users' opt-out preference signals, honoring these preference signals as valid requests.  
 
An authorized agent may submit an opt-out request on your behalf if you have provided the authorized agent signed permission to do so. All opt-out requests are processed within 15 calendar days from time of receipt.
